name: 21st Magic MCP

hlido_opinion.headline: A UI-component catalog turned into an agent-native surface — search, install, generate, audit and publish React components from the terminal or any MCP client, with the skills model doing the heavy lifting.
hlido_opinion.body: 21st Magic MCP is the agent-facing half of 21st.dev, a community catalog of React/UI components. Instead of a human browsing a gallery, the CLI and MCP server let a coding agent do the whole loop: search the catalog and read the real component code, install a component with its dependencies, sketch UI variants from a prompt, audit an existing page for accessibility and responsive issues and fix them, and publish your own components or themes back. The design decision worth noting is the 'skills' model — each job (find-and-install, generate, audit, publish) is a discrete skill the CLI loads on demand, and every action ships with a copy-as-prompt button that hands your agent the exact instruction, which is a genuinely thoughtful way to bridge human intent and agent execution. It works across Claude, Codex, Cursor and Lovable, with a global npm install and a browser login that saves a local token, plus an API-key path for CI. The honesty is decent: free search, two component installs a day on the free tier, and generation explicitly 'uses AI credits' rather than pretending to be unlimited. What holds it back from a higher score is that the surface is a capabilities tour more than a proof — the pricing is gated behind a sign-in click rather than laid out, and the quality of generated UI (the part buyers most want to trust) is asserted, not demonstrated with before/after evidence on the public page. For a coding agent that already lives in React, though, this is a well-shaped tool that meets the agent where it works.

tier_rationale: STEADY (79) because this is a mature, genuinely agent-native product — MCP server plus CLI, multi-client, with a well-thought-out skills-and-copy-prompt model and an honest free-tier limit stated up front. It is held below the mid-80s because the public surface demonstrates breadth of commands rather than evidence of output quality, and pricing is behind a sign-in rather than published. It rises with a public before/after of generated UI and a visible pricing table.
what_it_does_well: Genuinely agent-native: the same catalog is drivable from CLI or any MCP client, not a human-only gallery with an API bolted on
The skills model breaks work into discrete, on-demand jobs (search, install, generate, audit, publish) rather than one monolithic tool
Every action ships a copy-as-prompt button that hands the agent the exact instruction
Search reads the real component code and installs with dependencies, not just a snippet paste
Works across Claude, Codex, Cursor and Lovable with one global install
Free-tier limits are stated plainly ('Search free · 2 installs a day', generation 'uses AI credits')
Two-way: you can publish your own components and themes back to the catalog
what_it_fails_at: Pricing is gated behind a sign-in click rather than published on the surface
Generated-UI quality — the thing buyers most want to trust — is asserted, not shown with public before/after evidence
Value is tied to React/component workflows; teams outside that stack get little
The free install cap (2/day) is low enough to force an upgrade decision quickly
No named customers or usage evidence on the reviewed surface
best_for: React and Next.js teams whose coding agent should search, install and generate UI components without leaving the terminal
Agent builders who want a component-library skill that works across Claude, Cursor and Codex
Designers and developers who want to publish reusable components or themes for a team
not_recommended_for: Buyers who need published pricing before evaluating
Anyone who needs demonstrated output quality — not just a capability list — before trusting generated UI in production

compared_to.verdict_diff: Cursor is a full editor-based coding agent; 21st Magic is a focused UI-component layer that plugs into Cursor (and others) via MCP. They are complements more than rivals — Cursor for the whole coding loop, 21st for the component catalog inside it.

Claude Code is a general terminal coding agent; 21st Magic is a skill it can load to gain a component catalog and UI generation. Claude Code for general work; 21st as the UI-specialized tool surface it consumes.

agent_relevance.agent_integration_path: Native MCP server plus a CLI designed for agents. A coding agent installs the CLI globally, authenticates once, then loads discrete skills (search, install, generate, audit, publish) — each with a copy-as-prompt handoff. Works from any MCP client (Claude, Codex, Cursor, Lovable) and supports an API key for CI. The whole product is built to be driven by an agent, not a human.

Free tier limits stated (search free, 2 installs/day, generation uses AI credits) but full pricing is behind sign-in
Concrete CLI commands per job and copy-as-prompt buttons; multi-client install docs
